casos.comentario: This was a case of a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (predominantly embryonal carcinoma) which caused considerable debate regarding scoring. As in previous circulations some people had misinterpreted the presence of scattered syncytiotrophoblasic giant cells as choriocarcinoma, which requires by definition a bi-laminar component of both cyto and syncytiotrophoblast and has prognostic significance. It was emphasized that a large number of participants (153) had requested immunohistochemistry and that a relatively high proportion of people (14) had stated that the case was unsuitable for EQA. However, on a show of hands there was a strong consensus to score the case and to merge categories 1-4 as correct (which represented 96.1% of participants) with all the other responses (5-15) to be regarded as incorrect.

It was emphasised that these tumours usually occur on a background on treated conventional (acinar) prostatic adenocarcinoma. It was agreed it was an excellent educational case and of note only a handful of Participants in the audience had ever made this diagnosis in their own practice.

casos.clinica: Left testis tumour. LDH raised. Multiple mets. Specimen: Left testis. Macro: Left radical orchidectomy. Size of testis: 17 x 13 x 11 cm. Size of tumour: 13.5 x 12 x 12 cm. Solid, yellow tumour with necrosis. Immuno: reveals strong positivity for inhibin, Calretinin, Melan-A and vimentin. Germ cell tumour markers (OCT3/4, SALL4, HCG, AFP, Glypican 3), epithelial markers and S-100 are negative. The Ki-67 proliferation rate is approximately 5-10%.
casos.comentario: This case gave a history of metastatic disease and the features were of a Leydig cell tumour with areas of necrosis and vascular invasion. These features were deemed to be enough in the clinical setting to call this a malignant Leydig cell tumour, which scored full marks. The meeting discussed giving half marks to Leydig cell tumour but on a show of hands unanimously favoured 0. All other diagnoses also scored 0.

casos.clinica: Papillary growth in prostatic urethra extending into prostate. PSA 43 ? Ca prostate ? TCC of prostatic urethra. Specimen: TURP. Macro: Prostate chips weighing 75g. Immuno: PSAP strongly positive, PSA weakly positive.
casos.comentario: This TURP had large ducts filled with a cribriform cancer as well as fragments of solid cancer. The clinical history of a papillary tumour in the urethra was classical for ductal carcinoma and the PSA positivity meant that this was diagnostic of ductal variant of prostatic adenocarcinoma. The expansile nature, columnar cytomorphology and focal papillary architecture argued against intraductal cancer and PIN-like variant. Ductal cancers often have a microacinar component but this was deemed to be incorrect in this case.

casos.clinica: Mass in left testis. Specimen: Left Orchidectomy. Macro: Testis measuring 50x40x35 mm with attched spermatic cord measuring 65 mm in length x up to 25mm. Slicing the specimen reveals a solid pale brown tumour that measures 35x25 mm. Immuno: N/A.
casos.comentario: This was a straightforward case of seminoma submitted without immunohistochemistry, which many felt was required but still there was high agreement. Seminoma with syncytiotrophoblastic cells was allowed. All other answers were deemed incorrect.

casos.clinica: Robotic radical prostatectomy, PSA 10.5, Gleason 3+4 on biopsy. Specimen: Radical prostatectomy. Macro: Radical prostatectomy - 71grams. Cruciate block from base margin. Immuno: None.
casos.comentario: This was a cruciate block from the base margin of a radical prostatectomy and it clearly had prostatic adenocarcinoma but there was some confusion over terminology with some participants wanting to put prostatic adenocarcinoma but this was not a choice - it has to be noted that microacinar or acinar is the usual type of prostatic adenocarcinoma and this was answered by 95% of participants. We have edited the diagnosis now to state "Prostatic adenocarcinoma Acinar/Microacinar (Usual type)" The other variants were considered as incorrect. One participant put Other and answered in the comments box and the meeting felt leniency towards them and allowed them to score.

casos.clinica: History of left orchidectomy. Suspicious lump in right testis. Specimen: Right testis. Macro: Right testis measuring 65 x 40 x 45 mm with intact vaginal sac and 25 mm spermatic cord attached. Sectioning reveals a solid and cystic tumour measuring 40 x 30 x 40 mm confined within the tunica albuginea. Immuno: GFAP and NSE highlighted glial tissue and neurons. OCT3/4 and Myogenin negative.
casos.comentario: This was a case of pure testicular teratoma. A large number of Participants had commented on the relative rarity of this subtype of tumour in adults and the need for examining multiple sections to exclude other germ cell elements (the new RCPath 3rd edition guidelines stating at least 1 block/cm of tumour). A number of people had concerns about the presence of immature elements and it was emphasised that this does not have prognostic significance in testicular tumours (in contrast to their ovarian counterparts). The widespread atypia in the epithelial and mesenchymal components was against dermoid cyst and as this diagnosis would have potential serious implications for patient management it was unanimously scored incorrect 0. There was no pure overgrow of cytologically malignant mesenchymal or epithelial elements required for a diagnosis of somatic-type transformation. On a show of hands it was agreed to award this category half marks. Categories 3 and 1 were merged, as a number of people had requested AFP immuno to exclude a possible yolk sac component.

casos.clinica: Circumcision for scarring. Specimen: Foreskin. Macro: Multiple pieces of skin largest measuring 30x20x10mm. Two of these pieces show a firm white surface. Immuno: Nil.
casos.comentario: This was a straightforward case of Balanitis xerotica obliterans for which there was 100% agreement. Some people commented on the preferred term being lichen sclerosus et atrophicus and the diagnosis in the dropdown box will be ammended to Balanitis xerotica obliterans/lichen sclerosus

casos.clinica: Testicular swelling. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Enlarged testis containing a 60mm white-pinkish soft tumour.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
There was strong agreement that spermatocytic seminoma was the correct diagnosis, and that this was a diagnosis which could be made on morphological grounds, without the need for immunohistochemistry. It was agreed to merge categories 1 and 3 for scoring purposes. Seminoma? spermatocytic was not felt to be specific enough and merited half marks. Classical seminoma, seminoma and ITGCN and lymphoma were regarded as incorrect.

casos.clinica: Right scrotal mass. ?Epididymal tumour. No trauma. No urinary symptoms. Specimen: Right testis. Macro: Right testis, 11 x 7 x 5cm with white paratesticular mass 6 x 6 x 2.5cm. The tumour is lobulated and grey with haemorrhagic areas. Testis macroscopically normal.
casos.diagnostico: Extensive fat necrosis most likely secondary to infarction of a spermatic cord lipoma
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case generated a huge differential diagnosis. Over 20 participants indicated they would have referred this for opinion to a soft tissue specialist and a number indicated it was more suitable to a soft tissue rather than urological EQA. As a considerable number of respondents had diagnosed liposarcoma, which was at variance with the reporting Pathologist's diagnosis of fat necrosis secondary to infarction of a spermatic cord lipoma, the submitting Pathologist was contacted. The submitting Pathologist subsequently referred the case for further opinion. The Pathologist to whom the case was referred found this a difficult case and was not able to say with complete confidence whether it was benign or malignant. Reassuringly, the patient remains well at follow-up with no evidence of disease recurrence. The meeting unanimously agreed this case should be designated educational and excluded from scoring.

casos.clinica:
Painful left scrotal mass. ?Cyst. Immunocytochemistry showed strong reactivity for keratin (AE1/AE3) and Calretinin. CEA and CD34 were negative. Specimen: Left epididymal cyst. Macro:
Pale, firm solid nodule measuring 12 x 10 x 6mm with no cystic component on serial section. The cut surface was homogenous and pale.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a straightforward case of adenomatoid tumour. Sclerosing Sertoli cell tumour was regarded as incorrect by the meeting.

casos.clinica:
Presented with vague left testicular dull ache and swelling. Scrotal USS - multiloculat lesion lower pole left testis. Left radical orchidectomy done.
Specimen: Left testis. Macro: Testis, weight 36g measuring 45 x 35 x 30mm, spermatic cord 60 x 25 x 20mm, epidydmis 50 x 20 x 20mm. Tumour found in lower half of testicular parenchyma, grey white, multinodular with ill-defined borders measuring 28 x 20 x 20mm.
casos.diagnostico: Malignant teratoma intermediate (MTI) without vascular invasion
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
The difficulties of data entry with this case as a result of participants using either the BTTP, WHO 2004 or combinations of both classifications in their responses was pointed out. The organiser attempted to transcribe responses into the BTTP classification, as this produced the least number of diagnostic categories. Using this approach MTU was favored over MTI (the latter being the reporting Pathologist's diagnosis). There was 100% agreement this represented a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour and it was pointed out this was the most relevant diagnosis as far as the oncologist was concerned for treatment. There was a brief discussion as to which classification was superior. A slide was shown providing verbatim responses by participants, to highlight that there appears to be considerable confusion in terminology, particularly with usage of the BTTP classification. It was agreed that a future BAUP workshop should specifically address the issue of terminology in classification of testicular germ cell tumours.

casos.clinica: Solid lesion adherent to lower pole of testis. Said to be epididymal on ultrasound. Immuno: Positive for AE1/3. Negative for CD31. Positive for Alcan Blue (hyaluronidase sensitive). Negative for Epithelial mucin. Specimen: Lower pole testis/?epididymis. Macro: 10mm diameter firm pale nodule.

Meeting comments:
This was a straight forward case of adenomatoid tumour correctly identified by the majority of Participants. Category 2 (mesothelioma of the tunica) was regarded as incorrect for scoring purposes.

casos.clinica: Solid testicular and spermatic cord mass. Radical orchidectomy. Right testis. Immuno: CD10+ Mib1 - 70% CD19+ bck-2+ CD5 o53beg CD20+ CD79+ bcl-+/- CD23- MUM-1+FOX-P1+. Specimen: Right testis. Macro: Testis and cord weighs 173gm. There is a large cream coloured mass within the testis which measures up to 6 x 4 x 4.5cm. This covers most of the testis and is seen extending up the spermatic cord.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a straight forward case of a testicular B-cell non Hodgkins lymphoma, for which there was 100% diagnostic agreement.

casos.clinica: Mass replacing right testis. History of multiple myeloma. Immuno: CD138 + CD56 +. Specimen: Right testis. Macro: Testis containing solid white tumour 40 x 30x 25mm confined to testis.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a straight forward case of myeloma/plasmacytoma involving the kidney. It was agreed unanimously for scoring purposes to merge categories 1, 2, 3, and 4, as sub-classification was primarily the role of the lymphoma Pathologist. Category 5 neuroendocrine tumor was regarded as wrong.

casos.clinica: Left testicular tumour. Specimen: Left radical orchidectomy. Macro: Specimen consists of testis & appendages weigh 36gm. There is attached spermatic cord up to 7.5cm with testis 5x3 x2cm. On sectioning the testis there is a tumour which measures up to a maximum dimension of 1.2cm imdway down the testis to one edge. It is seen in up to 4 slices, giving a maximum thickness of about 1.3cm.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a case of a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) featuring embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumour, teratoma and syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells. Responses were translated into the BTTP classification simply because it produced fewer diagnostic categories. For scoring purposes it was agreed to merge categories 1, 2, 3 and 6. As with a previous NSGCT case, there was considerable inter-observer variation between those reporting choriocarcinoma versus syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells. There was strong agreement that category 5 (pure yolk sac tumor) was incorrect given the obvious presence of an embryonal carcinoma component both morphologically and from the immuno description provided and that category 4 that identified a seminoma component was also incorrect.

casos.clinica: Had orchidectomy following presentation with a testicular swelling. Immuno: Tumour cells diffusely positive with alpha-inhibin and vimentin, and scattered cells positive with Melan A. Specimen: Orchidectomy. Macro: Cut section of the testis showed a well circumsribed nodule with a uniform tan-coloured cut surface, abutting but not invading the tunica albuginea. The rest of the testis, the epididymis and spermatic cord were normal.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was another straight forward case of leydig cell tumor. A number of people identified focal mitotic activity, but overall most favored a benign lesion due to the lack of any other features associated with malignant potential (e.g. size, necrosis, vascular invasion, local invasion). It was agreed to merge diagnostic categories 1 and 2 for scoring purposes. 3 and 4 (metastatic adrenocortical carcinoma and sertoli cell tumor, respectively) were regarded as incorrect.

casos.clinica: Radical orchidectomy for testicular tumour. Specimen: Orchidectomy. Macro: Multiple pale nodules in testis and nodule on external surface of tunica.
casos.diagnostico: Mixed seminomatous and no-seminomatous germ cell tumour
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case represented a combined seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) with good agreement (92%). The meeting felt the embryonal carcinoma component was clearly invasive rather than in situ and therefore it was agreed category 2 should be awarded half marks. Categories 3 and 4 (seminoma and spermatocytic seminoma) were regarded as incorrect.

casos.clinica: Firm lump left testis ?tumour. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Testis 3.5 x 3 x 2.5cm with 8cm spermatic cord and epididymis, 2cm in diameter. At the base of the epididymis there is a firm nodule. On sectioning this is a 0.9cm solid cream nodule sampled in its entirety.

casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case caused a wide range of differing diagnoses although most favored a tumour in the sex cord stromal category. Large numbers of people highlighted the need for immunohistochemistry, which was actually performed but not provided by the submitting Pathologist. The favored diagnosis of the reporting Pathologist was that of a sertoli cell tumor but the case has been excluded for scoring purposes due to lack of diagnostic agreement.

casos.clinica: Hard mass upper pole left testis. Immuno: Thyroglobulin and TTF-1 Negative, Cytokeratin positive cells lining cystic areas. Remaining tumour vimentin positive and inhibin positive. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Cut section showed firm yellow area with gelatinous foci 30mm in diameter.
casos.diagnostico: Leydig cell tumour infiltrating rete testis
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case generated considerable discussion, but had to be excluded for scoring purposes due to lack of agreement. The majority of participants favoured a Leydig cell tumour (the submitting Pathologist's diagnosis) with a proportion flagging concern regarding possible malignant potential due to presence of pleomorphism, mitotic activity and extra testicular extension. It was noted that a small number of participants had misinterpreted the cystic transformation of the rete to represent a germ cell (teratomatous) component. It was highlighted that no clinical follow-up was available for this case.

casos.clinica:
Carcinoma of prostate, DXT, PSA0.2. Mass on CT causing hydronephrosis. TUR probably prostate. Immuno: PSA PSAP negative, TTF-1, CD56, synaptophysin chromogranin and CAM 5.2 positive.
Specimen: Bladder biopsy. Macro: 2g of curettings.
casos.diagnostico: High grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of small cell type
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
There was good agreement that this case represented small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma. It was emphasized that although with the previous history of prostatic carcinoma, this was the most likely primary, that clinical and radiological correlation were advisable due to the possibility of a bladder primary. A number of participants commented that TTF-1 is not specific for lung small cell carcinoma, as has been emphasized in previous EQA cases. Accordingly responses 2, 3 and 5 were regarded as incorrect. The meeting regarded category 4 (neuroendocrine tumour) to be too ambiguous and this was also regarded as incorrect for scoring.

casos.clinica: Patient had mucosa prostate urethra ?TCC, ?Inflammatory, stricture urethra. Specimen: Prostatic biopsy. Macro: None given.
casos.diagnostico: Prostatic adenocarcinoma large duct / endometrioid type
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case generated considerable discussion. There was good agreement (77%) that this was a prostatic ductal (endometrioid) adenocarcinoma. Quite a large number of participants (54) commented on the need for immunohistochemistry which was pointed out to have been performed on the original tissue at the time of original diagnosis, but had not been provided by the submitting Pathologist. The meeting felt that this diagnosis was tenable on morphological grounds. Categories 4 and 6 (urethral papillary adenocarcinoma and adenocarcinoma +/- ? primary/secondary, respectively) were felt to merit half marks and categories 2, 3, 5, 8, 9 and 10 were regarded as incorrect for scoring.

casos.clinica: Bilateral testicular tumours. Specimen: Right orchidectomy. Macro: 32mm tumour.
casos.diagnostico: Classical seminoma invading stroma of rete testis and epididymis
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a straight forward case of seminoma showing invasion of the rete testis with background intratubular germ cell neoplasia. Although 31 participants mentioned immunohistochemistry, it was the consensus of the meeting that this diagnosis was straight forward on morphological grounds and it was pointed out that immunohistochemistry was not performed on the original tumour at the time of primary reporting. Category 2, suggesting combined seminoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumour was therefore awarded half marks and categories 3,4, 5 and 6 were regarded as incorrect.

casos.clinica: Enlarged and hard left testis. Immuno: tumour is alpha FP and CD30 focally positive. Specimen: Left testis. Macro: Majority of testis replaced by tumour measuring 85x45mm. Cystic and haemorrhagic areas noted.
casos.diagnostico: Yolk sac tumour>90% and malignant teratoma undifferntiated (MTU <10%)
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case of a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour created considerable discussion. It was highlighted that as for previous cases, the responses were translated into the BTTP classification for ease of scoring, rather than personal preference over the WHO 2004 classification. An email had been received from a participant suggesting that all future responses for germ cell tumours should be using WHO 2004, but reservations were had as to whether the OMNIS software would be able to cope with the high number of combinations of diagnoses that were likely to be generated. It was emphasized that for this case the majority of the tumour was yolk sac in morphology and some participants had noted a minor teratomatous component. A number of participants had commented on the lack of obvious embryonal carcinoma in the section provided, but the presence of this had been inferred from the immuno description provided (CD30 positive). It was agreed to merge categories 1 to 6 as non-seminomatous germ cell tumour for scoring purposes, as this was the most relevant diagnosis to the clinician.

casos.clinica:
Lower pole testicular tumour. Normal tumour markers. Immuno: OCT3/4 &PLAP positive; CD30 negative. Specimen: Left radical orchidectomy.
Macro: Two nodules of solid white tumour in testis, each 12mms max. No haemorrhage or necrosis. Both appear confined to the testis.
casos.diagnostico: Seminoma, pT1 with invasion of rete testis
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
There was very high agreement that this case was a classical seminoma (99%). A large number of people commented on the presence of rete invasion and intra-tubular germ cell neoplasia. Category 2 correctly identified seminoma, although stating there was no invasion of the rete. As the morphological diagnosis was correct it was agreed by the meeting to merge this with category 1 for scoring purposes.

casos.clinica: Chronic pain left testis. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Testis 7x4x3cm. Within the epididymis there is a 1cm firm white lesion.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a case of a small adenomatoid tumour. Unfortunately, the lesional tissue had clearly cut out of some of the sections and there was accordingly very poor agreement. The importance of the submitting Pathologist checking that the diagnostic lesion is present in each slide prior to submitting a case was emphasized. This case was therefore excluded for scoring purposes.

casos.clinica: BPH clinically. TURP for LUTS. Specimen: Not specified. Macro: 50g of chips resected.
casos.diagnostico: Adenocarcinoma, Gleason 3+3= score 6 and also nodular hyperplasia
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case generated considerable discussion. Although the favoured diagnosis was Gleason score 3 + 3 = 6 adenocarcinoma (68%), because of lack of agreement for Gleason score it was agreed to disregard this from scoring and merge categories 1, 2, 3 and 5 which had all made a definite diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, which the meeting felt was relatively straightforward on morphological grounds. Categories 4 and 6 (suspicious for adenocarcinoma and adenosis, respectively) were regarded as incorrect for scoring purposes.

casos.clinica:
Left testicular tumour. Specimen: Left orchidectomy. Macro: Testis expanded by a nodular mass 47mm diameter with a solid cream cut surface.
Immunohistochemistry: CD43, CD20, CD79a, LCA, BCL-2 positive. CD5 weak, uniform in larger cells. Cyclin D-1 positive in most larger cells. CD23, CD30, CD10 negative.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case was for Education and Interest only and was a case of testicular mantle cell lymphoma, correctly identified by almost all participants.

casos.clinica: Phimosis. Circumcision performed. Specimen: Foreskin. Macro: Two pieces of wrinkled skin 50 x 22 mm x 25 x 20 mm. Some scarring evident.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This was a straight forward case of balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO). One participant; who had correctly diagnosed BXO, had raised concern of atypia in the associated inflammatory infiltrate and suggested performing immuno. The meeting consensus was that there was no morphological evidence to suggest a neoplastic lymphoproliferative disorder and that these further investigations were probably unnecessary, but it was agreed to merge this diagnosis for scoring purposes, resulting in 100% agreement.

casos.clinica: TURP for urine retention. Specimen: TURP Chippings. Macro: Prostate chips. Multiple fragments of prostate chippings measuring 8.0 x 6.0 x 2.0 cm and weighing 22 grams. All the tissue was embedded. Immuno: Immunostaining shows that these lymphocytes stain positively and diffusely using CD20 and bcl-2, and patchily in about 50% of the cells using CD43. They are negative with CD3,CD5,CD23,bcl-6, CD10 and cyclin D1.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
There was very high agreement (>99%) that this case was of prostate chips involved by a neoplastic lymphoid infiltrate, which most people interpreted from the immunoprofile provided was a B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. It was agreed that sub-typing was unnecessary for scoring purposes and therefore categories 1 & 2 were merged as lymphoma NOS. It was indicated that the submitting Pathologist would be written to, as the diagnosis of mantle zone lymphoma provided was at variance with that favoured by the majority of Participants, of marginal zone lymphoma and that this could result in different clinical management.

casos.clinica: History of left partial epididymectomy for painful epididymis with incidental finding of a nodule diagnosed as seminoma (13 mm). Now completion left orchidectomy. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Orchidectomy specimen including 5 cm of cord, testis 3.2 x 3 x 2.5 cm. There is an irregular yellowish white fibrotic area in the hilum (rete testis) containing suture material measuring 2 x 1.5 x 1.5 cm. Vague nodularity is revealed on further slicing. The remaining epididymis and testis appear unremarkable.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case of a seminoma with rete testis invasion generated considerable discussion. It was emphasized that there had been quite poor agreement regarding the type of rete involvement (stromal invasive versus pagetoid), which has potential relevance to clinical management. Furthermore, many people that correctly identified seminoma, had not mentioned rete invasion at all. An email received from a Participant stated that it was felt to be unfair to score the case in this manner, as a comment on rete testis invasion had not been specifically asked for on the response form. The meeting agreed that for scoring purposes categories 1-6 should be merged. Category 7 failed to identify invasive seminoma and was therefore regarded as incorrect, as were categories 8 & 9 which suggested a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour and mixed germ cell tumour, respectively.

casos.clinica:
Previous seminoma. Now swelling right testis.
Specimen: Right testis. Macro: 27 mm soft creamy white mass with area of haemorrhage.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case generated considerable debate. There was high agreement (82%) that this was a spermatocytic seminoma (SS) which was the reporting Pathologist's diagnosis. However, the submitting Pathologist did not provide the immuno results (that were performed at the time of original reporting) and immuno had been requested by a large number of Participants. Despite this, the meeting consensus was that the diagnosis of SS was tenable on morphological grounds. It was agreed to merge categories 1 & 2, although it was emphasized that although there was intratubular spread of tumour in the section, there was no evidence of ITGCN (which would obviously not be expected to be associated with SS). On a show of hands it was also agreed to merge categories 7 & 8, which had specifically mentioned SS but provided a differential diagnosis requiring immuno on the same diagnostic line, although some people in the audience that felt this was overly lenient. By consensus, categories 3, 4, 5 and 6 were regarded as incorrect.

casos.clinica: Testicular lesion. Specimen: Testis. Macro: Not provided. Immuno: OCT 4 negative.
casos.diagnostico: Malignant teratoma intermediate (with solid yolk sac)
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
As with previous testicular cases this case was difficult to score. The responses had been transcribed into the BTTP classification to try and limit the number of different categories of response. The consensus of the meeting was that this was a mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour which morphologically contained elements of YST, teratoma embryonal carcinoma and scattered syncytiotrophoblastic giants cells (not choriocarcinoma). The negative Oct-4 provided created considerable confusion as over half the participants felt there was an embryonal carcinoma component (that would be expected to stain positively with Oct-4). It was also felt improbable that only a single immuno stain had been performed on the case. A Participant from the submitting institution reported that the immuno may had been done out of interest, rather than diagnostic necessity, as immuno was not routinely performed in such cases. The meeting felt that it was appropriate to merge categories 1-4, 6 & 7 for scoring as mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour. Category 5 (immature malignant teratoma), which failed to mention any other malignant germ cell elements was by consensus regarded as incorrect, as was category 8 (malignant transformation in teratoma), which infers somatic-type transformation, which was not present.

casos.clinica:
? mass in left testis on ultrasound scan.
Specimen: Testis. Macro: Testis 55 x 35 x 25 mm with attached spermatic cord 60 mm long. Slicing reveals a well circumscribed tan tumour 9 mm in diameter confined to the testis.
casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case was correctly identified by all respondents as a lesion of leydig cells, but generated varying terminology including tumour, nodule and hyperplasia. It was felt that it was reasonable to merge all categories 1-4 for scoring purposes, as the terminology for such small solitary lesions is somewhat ambiguous.

About four years before had cystic/solid mass removed from epididymis. Now complaining of painful atrophic testis. Specimen: Orchidectomy. Macro: Thickened paratesticular tissue up to 4 mm, around much of the testis, it is probably separate from the epididymis. The testis itself appears normal.

casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case had been submitted as educational and was commented on as difficult by a number of participants. It had to be excluded from scoring on the basis of lack of agreement. Interestingly, the most popular diagnosis (papillary cystadenoma of epididymis) was incorrect. The submitting Pathologist's diagnosis was a serous borderline tumour of the paratestis. The major differentials were briefly addressed and provided some references of interest. It was agreed to continue to make all submitted cases (including educational ones) scoring cases, as this meant people had to make an attempt and were therefore more likely to learn from the case. Furthermore, one of the cases submitted as educational in circulation H had been used for scoring.

casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case showed a prostatic adenocarcinoma with a focus of ductal differentiation. As the presence of ductal variant does not directly affect management it was decided that categories 1 and 2 should be merged. Category 3, suggesting immunohistochemistry to exclude a TCC, was thought to be safe practice and was scored as 1. Category 4, just stating adenocarcinoma was thought to be too brief, though prostate carcinoma was probably implied, and was scored as a �. All other categories were more dogmatic in the diagnosis of carcinomas from other sites (TCC, bladder or rectal) and were considered to be incorrect. The Gleason score was given by most contributors, though this was not requested, and there was a wide spread of scores.

This was a case of an adult cryptorchid testis. casos.comentario:
Meeting comments:
This case was correctly identified as a renal meduallry carcinoma (RMC) by 90% of respondents. After considerable discussion it was the consensus on a show of hands to merge category 2 collecting duct carcinoma (CDC), on the grounds that it is a related, high grade and clinically aggressive tumour (although it was noted CDC is not associated with sickle cell trait, which was information provided in the clinical details). All other responses, categories 4-7 (infiltrating PD carcinoma compatible with urothelial origin, metastatic yolk sac tumour, No idea!! Will be glad to learn what it is, high grade urothelial carcinoma (?metastatic) and poorly differentiated carcinoma, respectively) were regarded incorrect.

casos.comentario: There was a plethora of terminology used in this case leading one to suggest a degree of uniformity in this area should be sought, having stated this most respondents used several interchangeable terms when answering this question. The submitting pathologist had sent this case for review and it was felt that it was too extensive to call Bowenoid papulosis and it was reported as carcinoma in situ. At this meeting, it was advised that no pathologist makes the diagnosis of Bowenoid papulosis alone as this was a clinicopathological diagnosis (multiple papules on shaft and sometimes on foreskin). Having stated this the majority of respondents putting Bowenoid papulosis had stated that clinical correlation was advised or as a differential diagnosis with CIS, as a result the meeting felt this should be merged with carcinoma in situ, high grade PeIN, severe dysplasia, Bowen�s disease, PINIII (the meeting felt that this was a typo), intraepidermal carcinoma (diagnoses 1,2,3,4,6,7,8,10) and all would score 1. Grading this as moderate or PeIN2 was scored half marks as the dysplasia was full thickness. Condyloma acuminatum scored no points.

casos.comentario:
Average 2.9/5
This case was chosen in order to assess the candidates� ability to assess and classify complex testicular tumours. The case was thought by examiners to be a good example of a mixed germ cell tumour.
Pass marks were given to candidates able to give a competent description of the components (embryonal carcinoma, immature teratoma, syncytiotrophoblast) and arriving at a diagnosis of mixed germ cell tumour or a differential diagnosis favouring mixed germ cell tumour.
Candidate adding value by observing lymphovascular invasion and intratubular germ cell neoplasia were awarded additional marks, as were candidates suggesting appropriate immunohistochemistry, suggesting the need for serum marker studies and making appropriate observations about the natural history of the tumour.
Candidates whose differential diagnoses favoured other forms of testicular germ cell tumour lost marks. Benign diagnoses and diagnoses of seminoma, lymphoma and metastatic carcinoma were given clear fails.
Most candidates approached this question very competently and offered sensible correct diagnoses with considerable added value. A small minority favoured inappropriate benign diagnoses.

This case was chosen as a good example of embryonal carcinoma of testis and the case gave candidates an opportunity to gain additional marks by indicating appropriate immunohistochemistry and correlating with clinical and epidemiological observations. In the opinion of examiners this was not a mixed germ cell tumour.
To gain a pass mark candidates had to give a competent description and arrive at a differential diagnosis of embryonal carcinoma or a differential diagnosis favouring this diagnosis. Additional marks were awarded to candidates able to indicate appropriate immunohistochemistry and suggest relevant clinical tests.
Candidates who diagnosed other forms of germ cell tumour were given borderline fails. Inappropriate diagnoses of lymphoma or seminoma were marked as a clear fail.
This case was generally well answered and the majority of candidates passed this question, with many adding significant value to their answers. A significant minority of candidates lost marks by inappropriate observation of other germ cell elements and a few candidates made confident diagnoses of pure seminoma of classical type.

casos.comentario:
Mean 2.64/5
This case was considered by examiners to be a good example of uncomplicated chronic pancreatitis, and the case was included to examine the ability of candidates to recognise the histological process and confidently exclude neoplasia.
Pass marks were given to candidates indicating a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis and giving a good basic description of the process. Additional marks are given to candidates considering possible aetiology and making appropriate clinicopathological correlation. Additional marks were also given to candidates who could confidently exclude the possibility of chronic sclerosing pancreatitis on the basis of the histological findings. Borderline fails were given to candidates lacking confidence in the diagnosis or resorting to immunohistochemistry to exclude other diagnoses. Clear fails were given to candidates diagnosing neoplasia.
This case was answered well by the majority of candidates, with many adding some value to their answers. Many candidates suggested chronic sclerosing pancreatitis and imagined features of this condition: in the opinion of examiners there were no plasma cells and there was no onionskin fibrosis. Candidates over-stating these features were not penalised but candidates who confidently excluded the possibility of chronic sclerosing pancreatitis were given additional marks. A very small number of candidates preferred inappropriate malignant diagnoses.

Incidental mass left kidney when scanned for aneurysm. CT suggestive of renal malignancy. Radical nephrectomy (left). Laparoscopic.

In its mid portion, slightly towards the inferior pole, is a tan brown, variegated tumour with focal fibrosis and haemorrhage, measuring 4.2cm in maximum diameter. It appears still confined within the renal capsule although it is bulging the surface. Special stains showed that the tumour cells do not contain glycogen or mucin (PAS negative). Rare scattered cells and occasional entrapped renal tubules are CK7 +ve, but the majority of tumour cells do not stain for CK7. casos.comentario: This is a lovely example of this condition. In the slide we can see a fairly well-circumscribed tumour that consists of cells that possess thick cytoplasmic borders, plentiful clear cytoplasm and large irregular nuclei. In places the cytoplasm appears more eosinophilic with a perinuclear halo. The tumour cells in this case were positive for c-kit and E-cadherin and negative for the proximal tubule marker LTA. The features are thus of a chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. This was called a grade 3 because of the hyperchromatic, enlarged and often raisinoid nuclei. These tumours represent approximately 5% of all renal tumors. They are slow growing and are thought to arise from the intercalated cells of the collecting tubules.

Meeting comments:
Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma was the most popular diagnosis (84%). It was noted by several people that CK7 immunohistochemistry was not provided. The main alternative diagnosis offered was oncocytoma, but the unanimous consensus of the meeting was that this was Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (the diagnosis also made by the submitting Pathologist) and was diagnosable on morphological grounds. Although additional stains such as Hales colloidal iron, additional immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy may be of value, it was not felt these were essential to make a diagnosis in this case. casos.diagnostico: Left parietal pleural biopsy - suggestive of sarcomatoid malignant mesothelioma.
casos.comentario: The differential diagnosis of this biopsy lies between a reactive mesothelial proliferation associated with fibrosis and chronic inflammation or a sarcomatoid malignant mesothelioma. The nodularity of the cellular proliferation and its sharp demarcation from the deeper less cellular fibrous tissue is suggestive of a neoplastic process. The degree of cellular pleomorphism is worrying but could reflect reactive atypia. There is however no complex tubulopapillary architecture or invasion of adipose tissue. I believe that the histological features favour a diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma but should be considered in the context of the clinical and radiological features before making a definitive diagnosis.

casos.diagnostico: Lung biopsy - diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia.
casos.comentario: The appearances are of a multifocal neuroendocrine cell proliferation showing in-situ growth within bronchiolar epithelium and infiltrative growth in the adjacent lung tissue forming carcinoid tumourlets. There are no histological features to suggest pathology that may have given rise to a reactive neuroendocrine cell proliferation. The appearances are therefore those of diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNCH). This is a slowly progressive condition with a relatively benign course that produces localized bronchiolar obstruction in the regions of the neuroendocrine cell proliferations resulting in features similar to those of obliterative bronchiolitis, as noted in the clinical detail. Carcinoid tumours arising in this condition are relatively indolent and usually show no atypical features, as is the case in this biopsy.

casos.comentario: The H&E section (64989) of this bronchial biopsy shows multiple tissue fragments in which both in-situ papillary disease and invasive carcinoma is seen. The papillary areas are defined by central vascular cores bounded by dysplastic stratified epithelium. Elsewhere, islands of pleomorphic cells are seen to elicit a desmoplastic stromal response in one of the fragments. This represents a focus of invasive carcinoma. In view of the lack of both keratinisation and intracellular bridging and possible acinus formation, this lesion is best regarded as a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with a co-existent in-situ papillary component. Interestingly, immunohistochemistry showed strong staining with CK20, focal staining with CK7 (64985) and no staining with TTF-1. This immunoprofile does not validate this as a lung primary.

casos.comentario: This virtual slide shows scattered fragments and a single large core of tissue taken from a lung biopsy. The majority of this core shows replacement of the normal lung tissues by an inflammatory process in which mixed inflammatory cells, particularly macrophages are seen throughout. Conspicuous foreign body giant cells are noted as lymphoid aggregates. Barely noticeable on this magnification (and thus annotated!) are refractile spherical organisms. These organisms stained strongly with Grocott (silver stain) and exPAS. They were negative for mucicarmine. The appearances are consistent with inflammation as a result of yeast-form fungal infection. Histoplasma is the most likely diagnosis as cryptococci are usually mucicarmine positive. Further microbiological investigations failed thus the diagnosis of histoplasmosis was favored on MDT review.

This case aimed to assess the ability of candidates to assess small needle core biopsies in the face of a potentially misleading clinical history. The clinical history of a left lung mass is the original clinical history provided to the pathologist who submitted the case. Candidates need to be able to assess histological abnormalities without bias from the clinical history.
This was a good example of an organising pneumonia with many characteristic features. Candidates were given a pass mark for a competent description of an organising pneumonia or a differential diagnosis favouring organising pneumonia. Additional marks were given to those candidates who suggested appropriate special stains (trichrome, reticulin, gram, DPAS, Grocott or ZN stain). Additional marks were also awarded to candidates seeking clinical correlation with history of recent ill ness, serology, microbiology) or offering relevant observations regarding possible aetiology.
Borderline fails were given for answers indicating a benign reactive process but not favouring organising pneumonia. A confident diagnosis of interstitial pneumonia was regarded as a borderline fail.
Any malignant diagnoses were marked as clear fails.
This case proved difficult to many candidates, with a few candidates allowing themselves to be misled by the clinical history and arriving at malignant or other neoplastic diagnosis.

This case was chosen to identify candidates able to demonstrate a sensible approach to pleural biopsies and the diagnosis of likely malignant mesothelioma.
A pass mark was awarded to candidates who were confident about a diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma, or who offered a differential diagnosis clearly favouring a diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma. Additional marks were awarded to candidates who diagnosed malignant mesothelioma but recognised the need to undertake additional immunohistochemical stains in order to confirm the diagnosis, and exclude the possibility of adenocarcinoma. To gain these marks candidates had to indicate a sensible and efficient immunohistochemical panel, which might include calretinin, CK5/6, BerEP4, TTF1 and WT1. Candidates making aetiological observations (asbestos) also gained marks.
Candidates favouring a diagnosis of adenocarcinoma, or equivocating between malignant mesothelioma and a benign reactive mesothelial proliferation were awarded a borderline fail. Candidates favouring a benign reactive mesothelial proliferation were given a clear fail.
This question was generally well answered and many candidates added value to their answers by discussing appropriate use of immunohistochemistry and correlating their diagnosis with the clinical context. A few candidates failed to recognise the infiltrative nature of the process and its malignant nature.

Pass marks were given to candidates who gave a good morphological description and considered either pneumocystis carinii/ jiroveci pneumonia or the differential diagnosis of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. Additional marks were given to candidates indicating the need for special stains, immunohistochemistry or PCR to confirm the diagnosis of pneumocystis carinii/ jiroveci pneumonia. Candidates seeking clinical correlation (was the patient immunocompromised) were given additional marks, as were candidates indicating the need to search for other organisms associated with immunocompromise- e.g. CMV).
Fails were awarded to candidates failing to consider the differential diagnosis outlined above, attributing the changes to heart failure or intra-alveolar haemorrhage, or making a confident diagnosis of malignancy.
Most candidates answered this question well. Just under a quarter of candidates failed.

Approximately 20% of candidates failed this question, either by lacking confidence by listing extensive differential diagnoses, or by strongly favouring malignant diagnoses other than malignant mesothelioma.

This disease, also known as Grönblad-Strandberg syndrome, represents a genetic disease that results in abnormal fragmentation / mineralization of elastic fibres in certain tissues. The skin and eyes are commonly affected.

Immunohistochemistry for HHV8 (shown here) confirms the diagnosis.

This punch biopsy shows skin in which irregularly acanthotic / hyperkeratotic epidermis overlies
focally inflamed dermis. At the dermo-epidermal junction, chronic inflammatory cells are seen in a
patchy, discontinuous, distribution with a relative concentration of cells at the base of rete ridges. In these areas the features are focally reminiscent of lichen planus. The surrounding dermis is somewhat sclerotic but otherwise unremarkable. This is the chronic / end-stage morphology of lichen planus.

This virtual slide shows a circumscribed dermal lesion composed of bundles of hyalinized collagen
separated by artefactual clefts with a storiform pattern. This is a storiform collagenoma.
This lesion, regarded as a solitary form of sclerosing fibroma, is characterized by the presence of dense collagen deposition in a markedly hypocellular but well-circumscribed lesion. Expression of CD34 (not shown here) is typical. It is suggested some cases represent the end stage of a folliculitic process.

This slide shows skin in which a crater-like lesion consists of epidermis in which supra-basal acantholysis is seen in association with dyskeratosis. This is a warty dyskeratoma.
Also known as isolated follicular keratosis, warty dyskeratoma usually occurs on sun-exposed skin. The lesion, characterised microscopically by follicular acantholysis and dyskeratosis, is possibly a primary proliferative process of hair follicles.

This case was chosen as a good example of a granulomatous skin lesion, testing the approach of candidates to necrobiotic granulomatous skin lesions. Candidates were provided with a helpful clinical history.
Pass marks were given to those who correctly identified the main abnormality as a necrobiotic granulomatous skin lesion and gave a reasonable differential diagnosis to include granuloma annulare, rheumatoid nodule and necrobiosis lipoidica. Candidates with a more confident approach and able to make a definite diagnosis of granuloma annulare were given additional marks, as were candidates offering clinicopathological correlation and aware of the different forms of granuloma annulare.
Candidates who recognised a granulomatous condition, but failed to note the necrobiotic component, were given a borderline fail. Candidates who did not recognise the granulomatous nature of this condition, or who clearly favoured leprosy or other tropical/ infective disorders were given a clear fail, as were candidates who considered malignant diagnoses.
This question was well answered by most candidates, with many candidates adding considerable value to their answers. A minority of candidates failed to recognise the necrobiotic component, or made confident diagnoses of tropical diseases such as leprosy.

This was a relatively straightforward case, aiming to test the ability of candidates to report an unusual but well recognised melanocytic lesion, and arrive at a confident benign diagnosis.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates giving a competent description of the lesion and clearly favouring a diagnosis of pigmented spindle cell tumour of Reed (Spitz naevus was also accepted).
Additional marks were awarded to candidates able to give a particularly good description of the lesion, commenting on the need for complete excision, or noting that the patient is older than usual for this diagnosis.
Candidates lost marks for equivocating between benign and malignant diagnoses, or arriving at clearly malignant diagnoses.
The majority of candidates were able to pass this question, but because of the nature of the lesion it was difficult to add much value to answers. Only a few candidates failed by offering equivocal or malignant diagnoses.

This case was selected to assess the ability of candidates to interpret non-neoplastic skin disease and consider infective aetiology. Candidates were provided with a helpful and relevant history. In the opinion of examiners this was a good example of Leishmaniasis, with clearly visible organisms. Candidates had to look at all of the material to be sure of seeing the organisms, which were not visible in all of the slices. This is a reminder to candidates to look at all of the material provided on the slide.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates giving a good basic description, including the observation of histiocytes distended by micro-organisms. To gain a pass candidates had to see micro-organisms and recognise infective aetiology, without necessarily diagnosing Leishmaniasis. Higher marks were awarded to candidates favouring a diagnosis of Leishmaniasis and indicating the need for Giemsa stain. Further marks were awarded to candidates able to add value by indicating knowledge of the natural history of Leishmaniasis, making appropriate clinical correlation with the history and indicating awareness of serological and molecular testing.
Borderline fails were awarded to candidates arriving at benign non-infective diagnoses. A fail mark would have been awarded to any candidate giving a malignant diagnosis. Only a few candidates failed to appreciate the infective aetology of the lesions.
This question was answered well by most candidates. Most candidates correctly identified micro-organisms, and a good proportion of candidates added value by correctly diagnosing Leishmaniasis. Only a few candidates mentioned the value of Giemsa stain or other ancillary tests.

This case was selected as an example of a clinically unexpected malignant melanoma, as can be encountered by any pathologist in routine practice. The case assessed the ability of candidates to diagnose and stage malignant melanoma, or initiate investigations to make an appropriate diagnosis. There was no appreciable intraepidermal component in the sections, and the lesion was minimally pigmented.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates confident to make a diagnosis of malignant melanoma on histological grounds alone, or favour melanoma in a differential diagnosis. Candidates who indicated the need for immunohistochemical investigations to confirm the differential diagnosis were also awarded a pass mark, provided that the immunohistochemical panel considered the possibility of melanoma.
Additional markers were awarded to candidates adding value by offering appropriate staging information (Clark level and Breslow thickness), comment on growth phase (vertical), staging, mitotic count, lack of intra-epidermal component hence the need to consider metastasis, appropriate subtyping as nodular melanoma, or awareness of the relevance of BRAF immunohistochemical staining in order to consider chemoresponsiveness. Other relevant added value was also considered on its merits.
Borderline fail marks were given to candidates giving a broad differential diagnosis including but not favouring melanoma.
Fail marks were awarded to candidates offering benign diagnoses, or confident diagnoses of other malignancies, without considering melanoma.
This case was answered variably by candidates. The majority of candidates gained pass marks by indicating the possibility of melanoma, supplemented by appropriate immunohistochemical stains. There were a few very good answers with considerable added value. A few answers were awarded borderline fails, by favouring other differential diagnoses, but suggesting appropriate immunohistochemical stains to consider melanoma. Only a few candidates made egregious errors, favouring inappropriate lesions.

This case was chosen to assess the ability of candidates to identify an important and common pattern of inflammation, and correlate with the clinical history.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates giving a good description of the lesion and favouring a diagnosis of leucocytoclastic vasculitis. Candidates offering clinicopathological correlation (association with prescribed medication) were given additional marks, as were those aware of the aetiology of leucocytoclastic vasculitis.
Borderline fail marks were awarded to candidates offering a description only, or identifying inappropriate benign diagnoses. Fail marks were given to candidates making diagnoses of malignancy.
Only just over half of the candidates correctly recognised the process and passed the question. Many candidates offered descriptions only or offered inappropriate benign diagnoses. A few candidates added value, by interpreting the histology in an appropriate clinical context.

This case was chosen as a good example of a relatively common melanocytic lesion that any pathologist might encounter in routine practice. The great majority of candidates passed this case with only a small proportion making erroneous malignant diagnoses. Malignant diagnoses were awarded a clear fail and candidates lacking confidence by offering broad differential diagnoses or noting the presence of atypia were given borderline fails.
To pass a candidate had to describe a pigmented and benign junctional naevus. Additional marks were given to candidates correctly identifying a pigmented naevus of Reed (or a Spitz naevus) and making clinical correlations with the age of the patient. This was a relatively simple case and it was difficult for candidates to score very high marks by adding value.

This case is from district general hospital practice and was submitted by a general practitioner. It is a good example of a lesion seen by many pathologists as part of day-to-day practice, and should not have caused any problem to candidates with good routine reporting experience.
Less than half of the candidates achieved pass marks for this case. Candidates lacked a holistic approach to the case, and did not identify organising thrombus in this case, or appreciate the reactive nature of the process. Many candidates favoured neoplastic lesions, and a small minority overcalled the lesion as Kaposi's sarcoma. The majority of candidates preferred benign neoplastic diagnoses.
To gain a pass mark candidates were expected to correctly describe the process of organising thrombosis, but not name the lesion as IVPEH or "Masson's tumour". Additional marks were awarded to candidates able to name the lesion and comment on the (non-neoplastic) process. Borderline fails were given for diagnosis of benign vascular neoplasms, and clear fails were given to candidates making malignant diagnoses.

This case was chosen as a good example of a blistering skin disorder. Candidates were assessed on their ability to arrive at a diagnosis and suggest appropriate immunofluorescent stains. Most candidates answered this question well and arrived the correct diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid: many added value by indicating the need for appropriate immunohistochemical stains. Some candidates failed to recognise the presence of eosinophils and favoured other less appropriate blistering disorders.
To pass candidates were expected to assess correctly the nature of the vesicle, comment on the presence of eosinophils and favour a diagnosis of bullous pemphigoid, as well as indicating the need for immunofluorescent studies. Additional marks were given to candidates able to make specific recommendations as to appropriate immunohistochemistry, comment on look-alike lesions and comment on the pathogenesis of bullous pemphigoid.
Borderline fails were given to candidates offering differential diagnoses including but not favouring bullous pemphigoid, or omitting to mention the need for immunofluorecent staining.

casos.comentario:
Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma are benign adnexal lesions which are, perhaps unsurprisingly, considered a variant of trichoepithelioma.
They usually occurs on the face, show a predilection for young adults and females, and typically present as sub-centimeter solitary firm lesions.
The tumours are usually dermal, well-circumscribed and are composed of nests and cords of basaloid cells with surrounding dense hypocellular stroma.
Distinction from the major differential diagnoses such as syringoma, infiltrative basal cell carcinoma and microcystic adnexal carcinoma can be challenging.

The specimen shows a central dermal tumour composed of large atypical proliferating T-cells. There is surface ulceration. In adjacent blocks, the epidermis shows extensive involvement with T-cells which form continuous clusters across lower to mid-epidermal layers.

casos.comentario: This skin shows mild hyperkeratosis. There is a lymphoid infiltrate in the upper dermis comprising mainly of CD4+ T-lymphocytes. These show marked nuclear atypia and there is focal epidermotropism. The features are suggestive of mycosis fungoides - A clonal T-cell population was detected by PCR confirming the diagnosis.

casos.clinica: Rash on trunk
casos.comentario:
The skin shows a nodular upper dermal infiltrate comprising of intermediate to large atypical lymphocytes. These cells showed an abnormal CD4+ phenotype. There is focal infiltration of the epidermis.
The features are consistent with plaque phase mycosis fungoides. But in view of highly atypical cellular morphology and pattern of infiltration skin involvement by a systemic T-cell lymphoma needs to be excluded.

casos.clinica: Skin biopsy
casos.comentario: The fragment of skin shows mild hyperkeratosis. There is a band link lymphoid infiltrate in the superficial dermis. This is seen alongside a perivascular infiltrate within the dermis. The infiltrates are predominantly of CD4+ T-cells which showed a normal phenotype. Similar findings were seen on a previous biopsy that showed T-cell clonality. Collectively the features are sufficient for diagnosis of mycosis fungoides.

casos.clinica: Lesion scalp: part solid, part cystic. Excised.
casos.comentario:
Mean 2.48/5
This case was chosen as a good example of a skin lesion which might be encountered by any pathologist working in a District General Hospital. Proliferating pilar tumours are regularly encountered in routine practice and it is important that these lesions are not misdiagnosed as squamous cell carcinomas.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates able to give a competent description, appreciate the pilar nature of the lesion and arrive at a diagnosis of proliferating pilar tumour or a differential diagnosis favouring this lesion. Additional marks were awarded to candidates adding additional value by stating that excision is not complete, understanding the histogenesis of these lesions and indicating knowledge of epidemiological factors.
Borderline fails were given to those candidates lacking confidence, equivocating between benign and malignant diagnoses. Clear fails were given for confident diagnoses of malignancy, or for diagnoses of pilar cyst NOS (and failing to appreciate the proliferative nature of this lesion).
This case was answered adequately by most candidates, with a few managing to add value and score additional marks. A minority of candidates offered inappropriate diagnoses of malignancy by diagnosing squamous cell carcinoma or trichilemmal carcinoma. Some candidates made inappropriate benign diagnoses, including pilomatricoma.

casos.clinica: Lesion scalp. Punch biopsy.
casos.comentario:
Mean 2.51/5
This was an intentionally difficult case, set to consider the ability of candidates to evaluate a spindle cell neoplasm of skin. There were some clues in the lower epidermis which might alert candidates to the likely melanocytic nature of the lesion: it would however be regarded as good practice to confirm this diagnosis immunohistochemically.
The marking scheme was set to reward candidates considering malignant melanoma in a differential diagnosis whilst at the same time considering other forms of spindle cell neoplasia of skin and using an appropriate panel of immunohistochemical markers to determine the final diagnosis. Candidates gained additional marks by indicating an appropriate and complete immunohistochemical panel or by providing a better than average description, noting the changes in the lower epidermis that might raise suspicion of malignant melanoma. Candidates favouring melanoma and noting the need to establish BRAF status were also rewarded.
Candidates whose approach was over-confident and who did not consider the need for immunochemical staining were marked down. Candidates arriving at confident diagnosis of other forms of spindle cell neoplasia of skin without immunohistochemical staining were given clear fails, as were candidates arriving at benign diagnoses.
Despite being a difficult case candidates answered this question well, with the majority achieving pass marks and a significant proportion of candidates also adding value. A few candidates lost marks by unfocused differentials, inappropriate immunohistochemistry (not including stains to consider the possibility of melanoma) and also over-confident diagnosis of other forms of cutaneous neoplasia.

casos.clinica: Itchy purple lesion, left wrist. Biopsy.
casos.comentario:
Mean 2.55/5
This was a straightforward case, set to consider the ability of candidates to evaluate an inflammatory process in a skin biopsy. Lichen planus is a common disorder, encountered in routine practice in most DGH Pathology Departments.
To gain a pass mark candidates were expected to identifying the correct inflammatory pattern (lichenoid) and to give a differential diagnosis including lichen planus.
Additional marks were given to candidates making a confident diagnosis of lichen planus and giving better than average description. Candidates indicating some clinical knowledge of lichen planus were also given additional marks, especially those candidates correlating clinical signs and symptoms with the histology.
Candidates describing an inflammatory lesion without noting the lichenoid nature of the process were given borderline fails. Clear fails were given to candidates who did not recognise this as an inflammatory dermatosis, to candidates arriving at malignant diagnosis and to candidates making confident diagnoses of blistering skin disorders.
This case was answered well by most candidates with many managing to add some value by better than average descriptions or clinical correlations. A minority of candidates failed to notice the lichenoid nature of the inflammatory infiltrate and a small number of candidates made inappropriate diagnoses of blistering skin disorders and neoplasia. The most common error was to fail to note the lichenoid nature of the inflammatory infiltrate and favour a diagnosis of discoid lupus erythematosus.

casos.clinica: Subcutaneous lesion left ankle. Excised.
casos.comentario:
Mean 2.36/5
This case was set to consider the ability of candidates to recognise diagnostic features in a difficult spindle cell neoplasm of soft tissue which retained some features of neurilemmoma, complicated by other degenerative features. This is a problem which will be encountered by many pathologists in routine practice.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates able to identify the features of neurilemmoma and give a competent description of the various histological changes. Additional marks are given to those candidates giving a better than average description and making a confident final diagnosis, indicating the need for appropriate immunohistochemistry.
Fail marks were awarded to candidates arriving at malignant diagnosis. Borderline fails were given to candidates offering broad differential diagnoses of benign lesions without a preferred diagnosis, or diagnosing other benign connective tissue neoplasms, especially myofibroblastic lesions.
This case was answered variably by candidates. A majority of candidates arrived at the correct diagnosis and some added value by offering good descriptions and appropriate use of immunohistochemistry. A significant minority of candidates were misled by the histological features and arrived at inappropriate malignant diagnoses. A few candidates lacked confidence and resorted to extensive differential diagnoses. There was a common tendency to over-state the vascular elements and conclude that this was a vascular neoplasm.

Disc of skin 48 x 47 x 10mm with central raised firm lesion 39 x 33 x 12mm. Note yellow ulceration in centre of the lesion 12mm in maximum extent.

Skin showing a large ulcerated multi-nodular tumour composed of a dense dermal infiltrate made up of a polymorphous population of cells. NEGATIVE in large cells - CD20, CD7, ALK1, CD15

casos.comentario:
These slides show a poorly circumscribed tumour which appears to be within the subcutaneous
fat. The tumour has an ill-defined infiltrative margin and is composed of plump spindle cells with central rounded nuclei and prominent nucleoli. There is marked variation in nuclear size and shape with some very large irregular nuclei noted. In addition there is an admixed inflammatory cell infiltrate composed of neutrophils and histiocytes.
Centrally the lesion shows large ectatic vascular channels, many of which have thrombosed. Prominent iron deposition is noted. Focal fat infiltration and dystrophic calcification is noted.
Immunohistochemistry (not shown) was positive for CD34, CD68 which highlighted many histiocytes. The lesion was negative for desmin, SMM, SMA, S100 and Melan-A.
The features are those of a pleomorphic hyalinising angioectatic tumour.
These tumours are regarded as indeterminate (locally aggressive) lesions with a tendency for local recurrence but no metastatic potential is reported.
Using a break-apart DNA probe which hybridises to the TGFBR3 locus at 1p22.1, the tumour cells showed rearrangement of this region with loss of the red (centromeric) 5' region. TGFBR3 rearrangements are reported in pleomorphic hyalinising angioectatic tumour.

Meeting comments:
This soft tissue case from the spermatic cord caused a considerable range of benign and malignant diagnoses. A large number of Participants indicated they would refer the case for specialist opinion in routine practice and it was therefore an unsuitable case for Urological EQA. The case was excluded for scoring purposes on the grounds of lack of agreement and was in fact reported as a dedifferentiated liposarcoma (the diagnosis having been corroborated by an experienced soft tissue Pathologist). It was emphasized at the meeting that lipoblasts are not a pre-requisite for this diagnosis. As the second soft tissue cord lesion in the scheme which had caused considerable diagnostic variation, the importance of seeking the opinion of a soft tissue specialist in these cases was emphasized.

Average 2.8/5
This case was set to assess candidates' approach to soft tissue neoplasms.
Pass marks were given to candidates giving a competent description of the lesion, noting characteristic vascularity as well as the presence of lipoblasts and arriving at a diagnosis of liposarcoma. Additional marks were given to candidates able to correctly classify this as myxoid or round cell liposarcoma. Candidates aware of characteristic cytogenetic abnormalities, the limited value of immunohistochemistry, the relatively favourable prognosis and the value of Trojani staining were awarded higher marks.
Borderline fails were awarded to candidates only mentioning liposarcoma as part of a list of differential diagnoses, without favouring the diagnosis, or confidently diagnosing other forms of liposarcoma other than myxoid/ round cell liposarcoma, or other forms of sarcoma.
Clear fails were awarded to candidates favouring benign diagnoses, of arriving at a diagnosis of "myxoma".
Most candidates answered this question well, arriving at confident diagnoses of myxoid liposarcoma. A few candidates were more vague in their diagnosis, and a small number of candidates thought that this was a benign lesion.

This case was chosen as a good example of a relatively uncommon but well recognised bone lesion, and aimed to assess the ability of candidates to assess a bone biopsy.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates able to give a competent description of the lesion and also able to make a confident diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia or favour this diagnosis in a differential diagnosis. Additional marks were awarded to candidates adding value in a number of ways; e.g.- by indicating the need for radiological correlation; an understanding of the epidemiology and natural history of the condition (childhood/ adolescence, good prognosis, usually cured by curettage, poly-ostotic vs mono-ostotic forms); knowledge of the genetics and the syndromes associated with fibrous dysplasia.
Candidates were awarded a borderline fail for an under confident answer that mentioned fibrous dysplasia in a differential but did not favour the diagnosis, or an answer that preferred other benign bony lesions. Clear fails were given to candidates favouring malignant diagnoses.
This case was well answered by the majority of candidates, with about one quarter of candidates adding significant value to their answers. Many candidates forgot to indicate the need for radiological correlation. A small proportion of candidates failed this question, usually by indicating alternative benign diagnoses, with three candidates indicating malignant diagnoses.

Average: 2.38/5
This case was chosen as an example of an unusual lesion that any well prepared candidate should have been able to recognise or at least describe and make a reasonable attempt at diagnosis.
A basic pass mark was given to candidates who offered a safe basic correct answer, describing a well-circumscribed lesion showing tri-lineage haemopoiesis, and offering a diagnosis of either extramedullary haemopoiesis of myelolipoma. Additional marks were given to candidates aware that a solitary lesion favours myelolipoma. Borderline fail marks were given to candidates whose answers lacked confidence and precision, identifying a benign lesion but without further added value. Fail marks were given to candidates who didn't recognise haemopoiesis or who offered confident diagnoses of malignancy.
The majority of candidates coped with this case adequately, offering good descriptions and correctly recognising the benign nature of the lesion. A few candidates appeared unaware of the lesion and made clinically unsafe diagnoses of malignancy.

This straightforward case was chosen as an example of an unexpected per-operative finding which any pathologist might be expected to interpret in routine practice.
Pass marks were awarded to candidates who gave a competent description of fat necrosis and arrived at a confident and correct diagnosis. Candidates who were able to make clinical correlation with the history of incisional hernia and likely entrapment were awarded additional marks, as were candidates giving better than average descriptions of the lesion. Borderline fails were given to candidates lacking confidence and resorting to broad differential diagnoses without a favoured diagnosis. Fail marks were given to candidates diagnosing metastatic malignancy or thyroid/parathyroid neoplasia, or categorically indicating that this is a benign lesion.

This lesion shows tumour lobules of variable size and form separated by prominent fibrous septa. The tumour lobules are composed of cells arranged as sheets and nests set within a myxoid to basophilic stromal background.The tumor cells have volumous clear to bubbly cytoplasm which contains small, dark nuclei.
Immunohistochemistry shows the tumour positive for pancytokeratin and EMA.
This is a chordoma.
Chordomas are thought to be derived from the transformed remnants of notochord and generally occur in the axial skeleton, commonly sacrum, skull base, and spine.
Brachyury (not shown here) is highly sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for chordoma.

casos.comentario:
These are core biopsies that show focal intestinal sampling but are generally dominated by a moderately cellular lesion comprising of spindle cells with elongated and uniform nuclei. The cells are arranged in fascicles and are embedded within a collagenous matrix. The lesion is seen to focally infiltrate the muscularis propria of the intestine (look at bottom right of the H&E). There is no nuclear atypia nor evidence of necrosis.
Immunohistochemistry shows the spindle cells to be positive for Smooth Muscle Actin (SMA). They are negative for
CD34 and Desmin (all shown here). Critically, the cells were also negative for S100, DOG1 and cytokeratin (not shown). There is some patchy nuclear positivity for Beta Catenin (shown here).
The appearances are in keeping with mesenteric fibromatosis.
Mesenteric fibromatosis is a locally aggressive mesenchymal tumour that may be familial in the setting of Gardner syndrome. They usually present as a deeply located slow growing mass that can cause compressive symptoms depending on the location.
